description.text: Sabbas the Sanctified was born in 439 in the Cappadocian village of Moutalaske near Caesarea. From a young age he was drawn to monastic life, entering the monastery of Bishop Flavian of Antioch at eight and receiving his tonsure at seventeen. He spent a decade at Flavian’s monastery before moving to Jerusalem and then to the strict cenobitic community of Abba Theoctistus, where he lived in obedience until the age of thirty.

After the death of Euthymius the Great, Sabbas withdrew to a cave near the Jordan and attracted a growing number of disciples. He founded the Great Lavra in the Kidron Valley in 484, later establishing the New Lavra near Thekoa to accommodate monks who preferred a semi-eremitical life. His leadership extended beyond the walls of his monasteries; he composed the Jerusalem Typikon, the first monastic rule of church services, and actively opposed Monophysite and Origenist doctrines by appealing to emperors Anastasios I and Justinian I.

curiosities.text: The spring that appeared at Sabbas’s lavra during a drought is said to have been a miracle, providing abundant water to the monks.
Sabbas’s relics were seized by Crusaders in the 12th century during the War of Saint Sabas and remained in Venice until Pope Paul VI returned them to Mar Saba in 1965.
The San Saba River in Texas was named after him when Juan Antonio Bustillo y Ceballos discovered it on his feast day, 5 December 1732.
